Heat is common but short. Rain is short and local. Haze is rare, but when it comes it covers the whole island and it can last weeks, as in October 2026.

We counted heat, rain and haze in NEA readings on data.gov.sg. Income wants a cover that pays when a public measurement passes a level. These counts show how often that happens.

Data we used

Work hours are 7am to 7pm, Singapore time. WBGT is a heat stress index that combines temperature, humidity, sun and wind. PSI is a haze index. A parametric cover pays a fixed amount when a public measurement passes a level. It does not check each person's loss.

NEA WBGT history starts in January 2025. Other NEA feeds start in 2016. All numbers are from scripts/heat_stats.py and scripts/hazard_stats.py.

Peril Measure Period Locations
Heat WBGT (heat stress), every 15 minutes 16 Jan 2025 to 7 Nov 2026 (661 days) 8 stations at the start, 30 at the end. Trends use the 7 stations that reported all period.
Rain Rainfall, every 5 minutes, summed per hour 16 Jan 2025 to 8 Nov 2026 54 to 90 rain gauges per day (median 61)
Haze 24-hour PSI, hourly 9 Mar 2016 to 7 Nov 2026 5 regions

Heat

  • WBGT reached 32°C, the MOM rest-break level, on 22% of days at a typical station. In the 7-station network, WBGT reached 32°C at one or more stations on 55% of days.
  • The heat is short. On 78% of station-days, WBGT was under 32°C for the whole day. A station-day is one station on one day. When WBGT reached 32°C, it usually lasted under 1 hour. Only 3.2% of station-days had 2 hours or more at 32°C.
  • The strong season is April to October, with 22 to 26 hot days a month. December to March had 1 to 15 hot days a month.
  • Location matters. Among stations with a full year of data, Sentosa reached 32°C on 58% of days. Tuas reached 32°C on 0% of days.
  • One app example pays S$50 a day, up to 10 days a year. It pays when WBGT is at 32°C or more for 2 hours at Bedok. The trigger was true on about 7 days a year. The premium is about S$11 a week. That is above the brief's "a few dollars a week".

Rain

  • A heavy hour is 20 mm or more in one hour, in work hours. It happened on 4.8% of days at a gauge, about 17 days a year.
  • At 10 mm the share is 10.4%. At 30 mm the share is 2.2%.
  • Somewhere in Singapore, a heavy hour happened on 36% of days.
  • Rain is local. On a day with a heavy hour, on average only 14% of gauges had one.
  • Rain is short. A gauge had on average 0.6 wet work hours a day. A wet hour is 1 mm or more.

Haze

  • From 2016 to 2025, the 24-hour PSI was above 100 ("unhealthy") on 0 to 6 days a year.
  • 2026 is different. There were 39 unhealthy days. 5 of those days were above 200 ("very unhealthy"). The peak was 230.
  • The main episode was 3 to 25 October 2026. That was 23 days in a row above 100. On 17 of those days, all 5 regions were above 100. Shorter episodes occurred in September 2026.
  • Haze is island-wide. On an unhealthy day, on average 3.5 of 5 regions were above 100.

What this may mean for our product

These four points are for discussion.

for discussion

Haze looks like the catastrophe peril

Rare, island-wide, and it can last weeks.

Haze looks like the catastrophe peril. It is rare. It hits almost everyone at once. It can last weeks. That fits a parametric trigger well. PSI is public. People already respond to it. It also brings the capital risk the brief warns about. It needs a cap on payable days and reinsurance.

From 2016 to 2025, unhealthy days were 0 to 6 a year. 2026 has 39 unhealthy days. The longest run is 23 days. On an unhealthy day, 3.5 of 5 regions were above 100.

for discussion

Heat at 32°C happens too often for a simple trigger

A duration rule, or 33°C, makes it rarer.

Heat at 32°C happens too often to be a simple trigger. A duration rule makes it rarer. One example is 2 hours or more. A higher level also makes it rarer. One example is 33°C. The employer rest-break cost per hot day looks small, because the heat is usually short.

WBGT reached 32°C on 22% of days at a typical station. Only 3.2% of station-days had 2 hours or more at 32°C.

for discussion

Rain is local, so basis risk is high

Use the gauge nearest to the worker or shop.

Rain is local, so basis risk is high. A trigger must use the gauge nearest to the worker or shop. If it does not, people will see payouts that do not match their day.

On a day with a heavy hour, on average only 14% of gauges had one. Somewhere in Singapore, a heavy hour happened on 36% of days.

for discussion

A bundle may work best

One cover, with a cap on payable days per season.

A bundle may work best. One cover can include heat, rain and haze. It can include a cap on payable days per season, as the brief suggests.

Heat at one location is 22% of days. Rain at one gauge is 4.8% of days. Haze at one location is 4.2% of days in 2025 to 2026, and 0.9% of days in 2016 to 2026.

Decide at the meeting

  1. Who do we insure: outdoor and platform workers, SMEs such as hawkers, or households?
  2. Which trigger, or which bundle?
  3. Who pays the premium: the worker, a platform, an employer, NTUC, or a lender?

Limits

  • Heat and rain cover under 2 years. That is two hot seasons, not "decades of history".
  • Haze covers 10 years, but 130 days have no data at the source.
  • The prices in the app are indicative only. A real price needs a longer back-test and Income's actuaries.
  1. Data source: NEA real-time APIs on data.gov.sg, https://data.gov.sg
  2. Scripts in the team repo ImNuza/sih-fin-4: scripts/heat_stats.py and scripts/hazard_stats.py.
